\paragraph{Severity scales with task difficulty.} Equation~\ref{eq:correct_conditional} reveals a counterintuitive property: sign misattribution becomes \textit{more} severe as the task gets harder. At $p{=}50\%$, $P(\text{correct} \mid \text{update}) = 50.2\%$---barely above random. At $p{=}5\%$ (a difficult task), only 5.1\% of updates are correct. Multi-turn agent tasks with low baseline success rates are precisely the settings where credit assignment is most needed, yet where step-independent training produces the worst gradient signal. Increasing $K$ does not help: it ensures more updates occur (fewer all-fail groups), but each update is equally likely to point in the wrong direction.

\paragraph{Reward saturation.} A complementary failure mode arises when all $K$ rollouts in a group receive the same binary reward. In this case, $\sigma = 0$ and $\hat{A}_k = 0$ for all windows, producing zero gradient (no learning). At $p{=}12.5\%$, the probability that all $K{=}8$ rollouts fail is $(1{-}p)^K \approx 34.4\%$. Combined with the rare all-success case ($p^K < 10^{-7}$), approximately one-third of training batches produce no gradient at all. This further slows an already compromised learning process.

Full derivations, analysis of why the community defaults to step-independent training (six contributing factors), and connections to classical credit assignment (TD($\lambda$), GAE, REINFORCE) appear in Appendix~\ref{app:theory_full}.
